meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Origin of a Theatrical Review: I Saw It Under Adverse Conditions. The Curtain Was Up'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Jean Nathan — his name turns up in 1968, decades late. Winchell printed it in 1931 crediting George S. Kaufman.

answer.label: Not George Jean Nathan — actually George S. Kaufman
answer.authorDates: 1889–1961 · American playwright, director and drama critic
answer.sourceLine: The first appearance Quote Investigator ↗ can find is Walter Winchell’s “On Broadway” column of 21 October 1931, and it credits George S. Kaufman, who had been asked how he liked Earl Carroll’s Vanities. Within a year the joke was being printed as Groucho Marx’s instead, and QI’s honest verdict is that the two of them are both plausible and it cannot separate them: “the jest was concocted by either Groucho Marx or George S. Kaufman.” George Jean Nathan is not in that argument at all — his name is attached to the line only in a Los Angeles Times column of 1 July 1968, thirty-seven years late.

source.heading: The earliest printing

docMeta.dd: Wisconsin State Journal, Madison, 21 October 1931, p. 3, col. 6

source.excerpt: Funny crack that one…I mean when somebody asked George S. Kaufman (who collabed on “Band Wagon”) how he liked the “Vanities” show…“I saw it under bad conditions,” he niftied, “the curtain was up.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the earliest instance as 1931 October 21, Wisconsin State Journal, “On Broadway” by Walter Winchell, Page 3, Column 6, Madison, Wisconsin, consulted via NewspaperArchive. The credit there is to Kaufman.

The Groucho version follows almost immediately: QI cites the Washington Post of 12 December 1932 giving it as Groucho’s (“I saw it under unfavorable circumstances. The curtain was up!”), and Winchell himself later said — in 1943, 1948 and 1949 columns QI quotes — that Groucho had told him the line.

QI’s stated conclusion is agnostic: it sets out two scenarios, one where Kaufman coined it and Groucho relayed it and one where Groucho coined it and blamed Kaufman to avoid antagonising the producer Earl Carroll, and ends “QI believes that the jest was concocted by either Groucho Marx or George S. Kaufman.” This page does not go further than that.

The George Jean Nathan credit rests on a single late source: QI records that it “did locate an article in 1968 that credited the drama critic George Jean Nathan” — Los Angeles Times, 1 July 1968, a column by Joyce Haber — referring to a Tallulah Bankhead play. Nothing earlier connects him to it.
source.excerptNote: Winchell’s column as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes it. Note the wording: bad conditions, not “adverse”. The “adverse conditions” form people search for today matches none of the early printings — the documented variants run “bad”, “unfavorable”, “unfortunate” and “peculiarly unfortunate”.

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted here. The exact wording people quote today — “adverse conditions” — matches no documented printing, so it has no identifiable first publication; and the earliest wording that is documented appeared in a newspaper column of 21 October 1931, which falls just after the 1930 cut-off for automatic United States public domain and whose rights holder we cannot identify. quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for this line.

author.name: George S. Kaufman
author.heading: About George S. Kaufman
author.metaLine: 1889–1961 · American playwright, theatre director and drama critic
author.bio: George S. Kaufman was an American playwright, director and drama critic who won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama twice — for Of Thee I Sing in 1932 and You Can’t Take It with You in 1937 — and wrote several of the Marx Brothers’ stage vehicles. He is the name in the first printing of this joke, in October 1931. Whether he made it up or was handed it by Groucho Marx is the part nobody has settled.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A perfect one-line pan travels faster than its author. This one has been assigned to four different men, and the assignment changed within a year of the first printing.

items.why: QI ↗ found exactly one source attaching the line to Nathan: a Los Angeles Times column of 1 July 1968, referring to “George Jean Nathan’s line about Tallulah Bankhead play”. That is thirty-seven years after the joke was first printed under a different name. Nathan was the era’s most feared drama critic, which is exactly the kind of name a homeless theatrical insult drifts onto.

Credited from the Washington Post of 12 December 1932 onward, and Winchell repeatedly said Groucho was the one who told it to him — a claim QI quotes from Winchell’s columns of 1943, 1948 and 1949. QI treats Groucho as one of the two real possibilities.

The name in the earliest known printing, Winchell’s column of 21 October 1931, and the name Groucho himself used when telling the joke, per the 1989 account in Peter Hay’s Broadway Anecdotes that QI ↗ quotes.

Winchell complained in May 1949 that Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations had given the joke to Woollcott. QI checked ↗ and found the grievance overstated: the Woollcott line in Esar’s book is a different quip about scenery, not this one.

misattribution.truthLine: On the documented evidence the joke belongs to George S. Kaufman or to Groucho Marx, and Quote Investigator ↗ declines to choose between them. It does not belong to George Jean Nathan.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The target was Earl Carroll’s Vanities, and the producer took it badly. Winchell printed the crack in his column, Carroll confronted him at a party in front of a room full of people, and Winchell was barred from Carroll’s theatres — “for nearly 20 years” by one of his own later accounts, “for the next 15 years” by another.
That is a lot of consequence for one line, and it is why the joke stayed in circulation: everybody involved kept retelling the story of the fallout.
detailsBody: There is a neat explanation for the confusion, offered in Peter Hay’s Broadway Anecdotes (1989). Winchell asked Groucho what he thought of the show. Groucho answered by quoting Kaufman — “You heard what George Kaufman said about this play, didn’t you?” Winchell printed it as Groucho’s. Hay’s version has Groucho eventually owning up to having made it up himself. It is a good story, and it is also fifty-eight years after the fact, which is why Quote Investigator reports it without endorsing it.

By 1934 the joke had shed its author entirely: Reader’s Digest ran it that December with no name attached at all, just “the critic who was asked his opinion of a certain play”. An anonymous joke is a joke free to acquire any owner, which is roughly what happened next.
context.pull: Winchell printed one borrowed joke and lost the run of a producer’s theatres for years.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator gives the first located instance as Walter Winchell's 'On Broadway' column, Wisconsin State Journal, 21 October 1931, page 3, column 6, which credits George S. Kaufman and reads "I saw it under bad conditions," he niftied, "the curtain was up."
QI cites the Washington Post of 12 December 1932 attributing the jest to Groucho Marx as 'I saw it under unfavorable circumstances. The curtain was up!'

QI concludes the originator is ambiguous, sets out two scenarios involving Kaufman and Groucho Marx and Earl Carroll's Vanities, and states 'QI believes that the jest was concocted by either Groucho Marx or George S. Kaufman.'

QI states it located an article in 1968 crediting the drama critic George Jean Nathan, citing the Los Angeles Times of 1 July 1968, and that when the quip is given an attribution it usually goes to Marx or Kaufman.
QI records Winchell being barred from Earl Carroll's shows over the joke, and quotes Peter Hay's Broadway Anecdotes (1989) on Groucho quoting Kaufman to Winchell and later owning up to the wisecrack.

George S. Kaufman was an American playwright, theater director and drama critic who won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Of Thee I Sing in 1932 and You Can't Take It with You in 1937 and wrote musicals for the Marx Brothers.
